First 2-part canon "super thema regium" from the Musical Offering. (Cancrizans)

source: http://javanese.imslp.info/files/imglnks/usimg/5/55/IMSLP10042-BWV1079-b.pdf

Original score denotes only 1 part on an alto clef. Alto cleff and key signature appears upside down at the end to indicate the retrograde.

comments.body:
Well, we have to talk about the context of the piece. I'm not a musicologist but I know the story fairly well:
Bach goes to Frederick, who tries to stump the old master and his "old ways," with the end result being the publication of this most glorious piece of music. 
Well, Frederick, the great king of the Enlightenment, was a man of science, who believed Bach's ways to be outdated. Essentially Bach was a kind of Leibniz optimist, the kind that Voltaire bitterly insults in Candide. Bach's music is rooted in an ideal that seeks not to communicate with man but with God, and so Frederick pulled a Voltaire attack on him, using the incredibly un-fugable subject. However, Bach, as a very authentic Christian (not the kind most people are nowadays, most of whom would reply with defiance), produces this extremely idealistic work to show Frederick that this is indeed the "best world possible, made by God for man."
Then we look at the score itself, filled everywhere with biblical references (see wikipedia, or better, read the books on the piece!). To me, this is an incredible religious and idealistic statement made to show the enduring power of Bach's beliefs.
